Praying for Others: How to Pray for Someone

Praying for others (intercessory prayer) means bringing a real person to God: you say their name, tell Him honestly how they are doing and ask Him to help them without dictating how. With the stories of Newman Hall, Hudson Taylor, John of Kronstadt, Ambrose of Optina and Elizabeth Wheaton.

By Lampada team · Published 2026-10-20

Praying for someone means naming them before God and asking Him to help them. Sometimes that is easier said than done.

The Alps, the Monte Rosa massif. This is how Newman Hall, a London preacher1, remembered one climb:

With my brother I was once climbing the Cirrha di Jazze, one of the mountains in the chain of Mount Rosa.2 When nearly at the top, we entered a dense fog. Presently our guides faced right about and grounded their axes on the frozen snowed slope. My brother, seeing the slope still beyond, and not knowing it was merely the cornice overhanging a precipice of several thousand feet, rushed onward.2 I shall never forget their cry of agonized warning. He stood a moment on the very summit, and then, the snow yielding, he began to fall through. One of the guides, at great risk, had rushed after him, and seizing him by the coat, drew him down to a place of safety.2

Back home, the brother heard something he had not expected: “On his return home, an invalid member of his congregation told him that she had been much in prayer for his safety, and mentioned a special time when she was particularly earnest, as if imploring deliverance from some great peril. The times corresponded.”2 Hall’s account appears in The Wonders of Prayer, a collection compiled by D. W. Whittle, and Hall was sure what it meant: “His life was saved in answer to her prayer.”2 In the same book Hall passes on another story: the friends of an organist who was gravely ill met specially to pray that he would live, and the very next day he started to get better3.

No miracle stands in for people here: the one praying was a sick woman far from the mountains, and it was a guide who grabbed the coat. But you can pray for someone from far away, even when the hand that reaches them belongs to someone else.

What is intercessory prayer?

Praying for others, which Christians call intercessory prayer, means bringing to God not yourself but another person: their name, their situation and your worry for them. Starting is simple. Say the person’s name. Tell God honestly how things are for them right now and what worries you. Ask God to give them what they need, whether health, peace, reconciliation, protection or faith, and don’t dictate to Him how it should happen.

For other things to bring to God, see our article on what to pray about.

Others pray for us too

England, the middle of the nineteenth century. His mother was away from home, and her son had a free day. By his own later account he was about fifteen; that afternoon he went through his father’s books, looking for something to fill the empty hours45. In a basket he found a small gospel tract. He took it for the story at the start and meant to skip the moral at the end4.

Meanwhile his mother was seventy or eighty miles away from him, and he had no idea what was happening in her heart4. That afternoon she got up from the table longing to pray for her son to come to faith4. “She went to her room and turned the key in the door, resolved not to leave that spot until her prayers were answered.”4 She prayed for hours, until she could ask no longer and began to thank God instead: His Spirit, she believed, had shown her that her son was already converted4.

When his mother returned two weeks later, her son was first at the door to meet her and tell her his good news4. She held him close: “I know, my boy; I have been rejoicing for a fortnight in the glad tidings you have to tell me.”4

And that was not all. Some time later he opened a little notebook by mistake, taking it for his own, since the two looked exactly alike4. It was his sister’s diary. She had written that “she would give herself daily to prayer until God should answer in the conversion of her brother”4.

The boy’s name was Hudson Taylor. He grew up to be an evangelical missionary, founded the China Inland Mission and gave half a century of his life to China6. Before he ever prayed for others, he found out that others had been praying for him, and he had never suspected a thing.

The man who turned away

Shortly before he left for China, Taylor had to dress, every day, the foot of an old man who was dying of senile gangrene. The Christian family the man lived with told Taylor that he openly called himself an atheist and was hostile to anything to do with faith7. When they brought in a Scripture reader without asking him, he flew into a rage and drove the man out, and when the local vicar called, he spat in his face7.

Taylor prayed a great deal for him, but for the first two or three days said nothing about faith and simply looked after him, taking care to ease his pain. When the patient began to thank him, Taylor, his heart trembling, spoke to him of his need for God’s mercy7. “He turned over in bed with his back to me, and uttered no word.”7 It went on like that day after day: many times a day Taylor begged God to save the man, after each dressing he said a few words, and every time the man turned away from him in silence7. One day, after dressing the wound and washing his hands, he did not go back to the bed but stopped at the door, thinking: “Ephraim is joined to his idols; let him alone.”7

The patient watched him go in surprise: until then Taylor had always come over to the bed before he left. Taylor could not bear it. In tears, he crossed the room and pleaded with the man to let him pray with him7. The old man did not turn away: “If it will be a relief to you, do.”7 Within days, Taylor tells us, the man accepted Christ7.

Taylor’s conclusion is not about the patient but about himself. Sometimes, he wondered, the real obstacle lies with those who are trying to help: their own hard hearts, and how little they grasp the reality of eternal things7. Notice something else, too. The prayer went along with the bandages, not instead of them. And Taylor prayed with the man only once the man agreed.

When you’d rather not pray for them

All of Russia knew John of Kronstadt, an Orthodox priest: crowds of thousands came out to meet him, and people revered him as a man of prayer8. Yet the diary he kept for himself shows an ordinary man whose feelings had been hurt: “I hear that the elder of the Gethsemane Skete near the Sergius Lavra, Father Barnabas, has spoken unkindly of me. What have I done to him? I must pray that the Lord will reconcile our hearts”910.

He does not ask God to set Barnabas straight. He asks Him to reconcile their hearts, both of them, his own included. The diary does not say how it ended.

Right after that comes another entry. The wife of a man who had once been his secretary came to see him and was rude to him, after all the help he had given their family11. “I confess I could not stand it and sharply asked her to leave my house”9.

Jesus said, “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44)12. John’s diary shows what that looks like in a real person’s life: praying for someone who hurt you starts with being honest about the hurt and asking God to change your own heart.

When the person is far away

People traveled to Optina Monastery to ask Elder Ambrose for advice, and those who could not come wrote to him; Dostoevsky took him as a model for the elder Zosima13. One day a letter came to him from a mother whose son had abandoned his faith. She blamed herself for not bringing him up as she should have, and she admitted that in her grief she had sometimes thought he would be better off dead than living as he was14. She asked whether she should write to him in Moscow on the off chance it would reach him, and how to word the letter so that it would touch his heart14.

His reply is dated November 22, 186914. Ambrose did not want her to take all the blame on herself: “every person is endowed with free will and will have to answer before God above all for himself”15. As for her main question, how to write to him, the elder answered: “But first, I repeat, you need to find out where he is at present and what his circumstances are”15. And then: “you should now be concerned not so much with bringing him to his senses as with praying for him, so that the Lord Himself, by ways known to Him, may bring him to his senses”15. And one more thing: “And while you pray for your son, pray for yourself as well”15.

We don’t know how the story ended. What remains is the advice: less of your own script, more trust.

That is how Jesus prayed for Peter on the eve of his denial: “But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32)16. Knowing that Peter would deny Him, Jesus prays for Peter’s faith and for his return.

Prayer and action

Elizabeth Wheaton was known as “Mother Wheaton”; for more than twenty years she traveled from prison to prison with the gospel17. In 1898, in a city jail, she met a young man under sentence of death, and his case stayed with her. When she looked into it, she learned that he had not even been charged with murder and did not deserve to die18. “I plead to God if there was nothing the law could find in him worthy of death, that his sentence might be commuted, and the poor boy might live.”18 She did not stop at prayer. Back from her travels, she went to see the governor in the state capital and asked him to change the boy’s sentence to life in prison18. She got what she asked for, and the boy was allowed to live18.

In 1899 she visited two condemned men the day before their execution. She talked with them and sang their favorite hymns with them, and then, as she remembered it:

we three kneeled together in prayer in the little “condemned cell.”19 Kneeling between my boys, clasping each by the hand, we gave ourselves to the blessed Savior…19

The two men sang and prayed all night, and in the morning they “went to the scaffold singing and praising God”19. This time her story has no governor and no reprieve.

For her, prayer and action went together. But prayer is not a lever that can move any decision you like. Sometimes the whole answer is that on their last night a person is not alone.

How to pray for someone

If you don’t know how the person is doing, find out first; that is where Ambrose began. Ask for what is good for them, not for your own plan. And if you have no idea what to ask for, remember the American preacher S. D. Gordon: in Quiet Talks on Prayer he admits that he is often unsure what to ask, since he may not know all the facts about a person20, and then he prays like this: “Blessed Spirit, pray in me the prayer Thou art praying for this man”20.

Put yourself into the prayer too: “reconcile our hearts.” For someone who hurt you, start with one honest sentence. If you lose your temper with them again tomorrow, so did John of Kronstadt. But praying for someone who hurt you does not cancel out boundaries, protection or your right to ask for help: from the people close to you, a pastor or priest, a professional, and, if you are being threatened, the police.

If you can help in practical ways, help. Offer to pray together, and wait until the person says yes.

Coming back to the person

In Lampada, the topic of a prayer is one sentence in your own words, and it can be a person: “For Mom before her surgery,” “For Andrew, after our fight.” You can answer the guiding questions by typing or by voice, and you don’t have to turn on the AI at all. If you have allowed the app to send your topic, Lampada will find Scripture passages that fit its meaning and will try to find ones about God’s care for the person you are praying for. You can listen to them read by a narrator and tap Save to keep them.

At the end you write a takeaway of a line or two. The journal is stored only on your phone, and search looks through topics, answers and takeaways. Type the name the way you wrote it, and search will find the entries where it appears in the topic, the answers or the takeaway, so you can see when you prayed and what you asked for. That is your own version of Taylor’s sister’s notebook. You can send an entry with the Share button, but whether to tell the person you are praying for them is up to you.

What Lampada doesn’t have: a separate list of the people you pray for, a way to mark a prayer as answered, shared prayer requests, or a community where you can ask others to pray. A standing list of names is easier to keep in a notebook.

Taylor found his sister’s notebook by accident. Perhaps someone is praying for you the same way, and you have no idea. Taylor himself would later write that from the very start of his Christian life he came to feel that “prayer was in sober matter of fact transacting business with God, whether on one's own behalf or on behalf of those for whom one sought His blessing”4.

Frequently asked questions

What is intercessory prayer?

It is prayer for another person: you ask God not for yourself but for them. The Gospels give an example: Jesus prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32)16.

Can I pray for someone who hurt me?

Yes. Jesus tells us plainly to pray for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44)12. When he was hurt, John of Kronstadt prayed “that the Lord will reconcile our hearts”9. But prayer does not cancel out boundaries or protection.

Should I tell someone I’m praying for them?

You don’t have to. Taylor learned of his sister’s prayers only when he opened someone else’s notebook by mistake, thinking it was his own4. But when Taylor wanted to pray with the sick man, he asked his permission, and the man agreed7.
